title: The Pale Blue Dot
hook: From six billion kilometres away, Earth is smaller than a single pixel.
peek: In 1990 Voyager 1 turned its camera back toward home and photographed Earth from about six billion kilometres away. Our whole planet shows up as a speck caught in a band of scattered sunlight.
lede: On 14 February 1990, Voyager 1 was about six billion kilometres from the Sun when it turned its camera around. It took a series of images of the planets, a family portrait of the solar system. In one frame, Earth is a pale speck taking up less than a pixel, sitting in a streak of sunlight scattered inside the camera.

bullets.text: Sagan pushed NASA for years to take the photo. Some argued it had little scientific value and that pointing the camera near the Sun risked damaging it. Soon after, Voyager's cameras were switched off for good to save power.

The full mosaic caught six planets: Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Mercury was lost in the Sun's glare, Mars in sunlight scattered inside the camera, and Pluto was too small and faint to show.
Sagan named his book Pale Blue Dot after the image. Writing about the speck, he said: "That's here. That's home. That's us." The passage is among the most quoted things he ever wrote.
For the photo's 30th anniversary, NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory released a reprocessed version using modern image software, keeping Earth as the same tiny speck in its band of light.
